lessonTitle: Acute Abdominal Pain: Localising, Investigating and Resuscitating

blocks.text: A 19-year-old sits on the edge of the bed in the emergency department. Twelve hours ago he felt vague discomfort around his umbilicus and lost his appetite; now the pain has settled low on the right and he winces when the trolley is bumped. The same hands-on question, where did the pain start and where is it now, is the single most useful part of the assessment.

blocks.markdown: Abdominal pain arises through three mechanisms. **Visceral pain** comes from stretch or inflammation of a hollow organ and is carried by autonomic afferents bilaterally to the spinal cord, so it is dull, poorly localised and felt in the midline at the dermatome of the embryological origin: foregut structures (stomach, duodenum, gallbladder, pancreas) in the epigastrium, midgut structures (small bowel, appendix, right colon) around the umbilicus, hindgut structures (left colon, rectum) in the suprapubic region. **Parietal (somatic) pain** arises when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which is supplied by somatic spinal nerves; it is sharp, constant, localised and worse on movement or coughing. **Referred pain** is felt at a distant site that shares spinal segments, for example gallbladder inflammation causing right shoulder-tip pain through diaphragmatic irritation (phrenic nerve, C3-C5).

blocks.title: Peritonism and peritonitis
blocks.text: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, most often from bacterial contamination (perforation, appendicitis, ischaemic bowel) or chemical irritation (gastric acid, bile). Peritonism is the set of examination signs it produces: tenderness, guarding (voluntary or involuntary muscle contraction), rebound tenderness and, when generalised, a rigid 'board-like' abdomen with the patient lying still.

blocks.markdown: **Taking the pain history.** Ask about site, onset (sudden suggests perforation, torsion or vascular catastrophe; gradual suggests inflammation), character (colicky pain comes in waves from obstruction of a hollow tube, constant pain from inflammation or peritonism), radiation, severity, time course, and what makes it better or worse (patients with peritonitis lie still; patients with colic writhe). Add associated vomiting, bowel habit, urinary symptoms, fever, jaundice, gynaecological history (last menstrual period in any woman of reproductive age), past surgery and medication including NSAIDs and anticoagulants.

blocks.caption: Pain pattern and likely source (illustrative, not exhaustive)
rows: Periumbilical then right iliac fossa (RIF)
Appendicitis
Anorexia, low-grade fever, localised RIF peritonism
Right upper quadrant, constant over hours, right shoulder-tip radiation
Acute cholecystitis
Fever, tenderness with arrest of inspiration on palpation (Murphy's sign)
Sudden severe epigastric pain spreading to whole abdomen
Perforated peptic ulcer
Rigid abdomen, patient still, tachycardia; history of NSAIDs or ulcer
Colicky RUQ pain lasting under hours, settling
Biliary colic
No fever or peritonism; normal inflammatory markers
Pain out of proportion to signs, atrial fibrillation
Mesenteric ischaemia
Early lactate rise; may have little tenderness at first

blocks.title: Scoring suspected appendicitis with the Alvarado score
blocks.prompt: The Alvarado score (MANTRELS) is one clinical aid to estimate the likelihood of appendicitis: Migration of pain to RIF 1, Anorexia 1, Nausea or vomiting 1, Tenderness in RIF 2, Rebound tenderness 1, Elevated temperature (above 37.3 degrees C) 1, Leucocytosis (above 10 x 10^9/L) 2, Shift to the left (neutrophils above 75%) 1; maximum 10. Score a 31-year-old woman with pain that began around the umbilicus and moved to the RIF, who has no appetite and has not vomited, with RIF tenderness, no rebound, temperature 37.8 degrees C, white cell count 9.4 x 10^9/L and neutrophils 78%.

steps.text: Migration of pain to RIF is present: 1 point.
Anorexia is present: 1 point. No vomiting or nausea reported: 0 points.
RIF tenderness is present: 2 points. No rebound: 0 points.
White cell count 9.4 does not exceed 10: 0 points. Neutrophils 78% exceed 75%: 1 point.

blocks.answer: Alvarado score 6: appendicitis possible. This is an intermediate score, so it supports observation and imaging rather than discharge; local cut-offs vary and the score never replaces clinical judgement.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing investigations.** Bloods in nearly every acute abdomen: full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C-reactive protein, liver function tests, amylase or lipase, venous blood gas with lactate, group and save (cross-match if bleeding or going to theatre), and a clotting screen if jaundiced or anticoagulated. Urine dipstick, and a pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age before imaging or surgery, because ectopic pregnancy mimics appendicitis. Imaging is chosen to answer a question: ultrasound for the gallbladder, the pelvis and (especially in children and women) the appendix; erect chest radiograph for free subdiaphragmatic gas; contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis when the diagnosis is unclear, the patient is older, or perforation or ischaemia is suspected.

blocks.caption: Targeted investigation by suspected diagnosis
rows: Appendicitis
FBC, CRP, urine, pregnancy test; ultrasound or CT
Raised white cells and CRP; non-compressible, dilated appendix with surrounding fat stranding
Acute cholecystitis
FBC, CRP, LFTs; ultrasound
Gallstones, thickened gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign
Perforation of a hollow viscus
Erect chest radiograph; CT if stable
Free gas under the diaphragm; extraluminal gas and fluid on CT

blocks.title: Do not delay resuscitation for a scan
blocks.text: In a patient with generalised peritonitis and haemodynamic compromise, imaging must never delay fluids, antibiotics and senior surgical review. Older patients and those on steroids or immunosuppressants may have blunted signs and a deceptively benign abdomen despite perforation.

blocks.caption: Values persistently above about 0.9 to 1.0 suggest significant physiological compromise (normal is roughly 0.5 to 0.7).

blocks.title: Resuscitation targets in a patient with a perforated viscus
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old man weighing 75 kg has generalised peritonitis from a perforated diverticulum. Heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg. After a urinary catheter is placed, you want a urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h. Calculate his shock index and the minimum hourly urine output you would accept.

steps.text: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure.
A value above 1 indicates significant compromise, so he needs prompt fluid resuscitation alongside urgent surgical assessment.
Minimum urine output is 0.5 mL per kg per hour multiplied by body weight.

blocks.answer: Shock index about 1.3 (compromised); target urine output at least about 38 mL/h.

items: Airway, breathing, circulation: high-flow oxygen if hypoxic, two large-bore cannulae, bloods including lactate and cultures.
Fluid resuscitation: an initial crystalloid bolus of 250 to 500 mL given over 15 minutes or less, then reassess, rather than a fixed large volume.
Early broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gut organisms, following local policy, for suspected peritonitis or sepsis.
Analgesia titrated intravenously and an antiemetic; nil by mouth and a urinary catheter for hourly output.
Urgent senior surgical review, with anaesthetic and theatre teams alerted in parallel.

blocks.title: Surgical decision-making in peritonitis
blocks.text: Generalised peritonitis from a perforated viscus requires source control, usually by laparotomy or laparoscopy, after resuscitation that is optimised but not prolonged. Localised disease such as uncomplicated appendicitis or cholecystitis in a stable patient can proceed to early surgery or, for selected patients, antibiotics first. The decision combines physiology, examination, imaging and comorbidity, and is made by a senior surgeon.

points: Visceral pain is vague and midline by embryological origin; parietal pain is sharp, localised and worse on movement.
A good pain history (site, onset, character, radiation, migration) localises the source before any test is requested.
Choose blood tests and imaging to answer a specific question; test pregnancy in women of reproductive age.
Generalised peritonitis with shock needs parallel resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent senior surgical review, not prolonged imaging.

questions.stem: In early acute appendicitis, vague pain is felt around the umbilicus. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The appendix is a midgut structure, so visceral afferents refer pain to the periumbilical dermatome
The parietal peritoneum is inflamed and supplied by somatic nerves at the umbilicus
Pain is referred via the phrenic nerve to the umbilicus
The appendix lies directly beneath the umbilicus

questions.correctOptionText: The appendix is a midgut structure, so visceral afferents refer pain to the periumbilical dermatome

distractorRationale.a: Correct: visceral pain from a midgut structure is felt in the midline around the umbilicus.
distractorRationale.b: Parietal peritoneal involvement produces later, localised RIF pain, not the early vague pain.
distractorRationale.c: Phrenic referral produces shoulder-tip pain, not umbilical pain.
distractorRationale.d: The appendix usually lies in the right iliac fossa; the site of pain reflects embryology, not position.

questions.explanation: Early appendiceal pain is visceral, travelling in autonomic afferents bilaterally to the spinal cord at the midgut dermatome, which is why it is felt periumbilically. When the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum the pain localises to the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 36 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain with fever 38.4 degrees C. On palpation under the right costal margin she stops inspiring abruptly. Which first-line imaging is most appropriate?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound
Plain supine abdominal radiograph
Barium meal
Erect chest radiograph only

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ultrasound is first-line for suspected acute cholecystitis, showing stones and wall thickening.
distractorRationale.b: Most gallstones are radiolucent, so a plain film has poor yield.
distractorRationale.c: A barium study is not an emergency test and is contraindicated if perforation is possible.
distractorRationale.d: An erect chest film looks for free gas and would not assess the gallbladder.

questions.explanation: The picture is acute cholecystitis with a positive Murphy's sign. Ultrasound is fast, bedside, radiation-free and demonstrates gallstones, a thick-walled gallbladder and pericholecystic fluid.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 8 hours of RIF pain and nausea. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Before imaging or any decision for surgery, which test is essential?

options.text: Urine or serum pregnancy test
Serum amylase
Serum calcium
Blood cultures only

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ectopic pregnancy must be excluded and it changes imaging and management.
distractorRationale.b: Amylase screens for pancreatitis, not the leading concern here.
distractorRationale.c: Calcium is unrelated to this presentation.
distractorRationale.d: Cultures do not address the immediate diagnostic gap.

questions.explanation: In any woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain, pregnancy status must be established because a ruptured ectopic pregnancy mimics appendicitis and is immediately life-threatening. It also influences radiation exposure and drug choice.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has sudden severe abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen, heart rate 122/min and blood pressure 88/50 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.text: Intravenous access, bloods and lactate, a fluid bolus, antibiotics, analgesia and urgent senior surgical review
Oral analgesia and discharge with outpatient ultrasound
Wait for CT to be reported before starting any treatment
Give laxatives and observe overnight

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous access, bloods and lactate, a fluid bolus, antibiotics, analgesia and urgent senior surgical review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: parallel resuscitation with early source-control planning.
distractorRationale.b: Unsafe for a shocked patient with peritonitis.
distractorRationale.c: Treatment must not wait for imaging in a physiologically unstable patient.
distractorRationale.d: Laxatives are contraindicated in suspected perforation.

questions.explanation: A rigid abdomen with tachycardia and hypotension signals generalised peritonitis, probably from perforation. Resuscitation, antibiotics and surgical review happen in parallel, and imaging only proceeds if it will not delay definitive care.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone has 18 hours of lower abdominal pain. She is tachycardic but her abdomen is only mildly tender without guarding. Her erect chest radiograph is normal. What is the best next step?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis with resuscitation, because steroids blunt signs and a normal chest film does not exclude perforation
Discharge, because the abdomen is soft and the chest film is normal
Stop all investigation and operate immediately without resuscitation
Repeat the chest radiograph in 48 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis with resuscitation, because steroids blunt signs and a normal chest film does not exclude perforation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: signs may be masked and the film is insensitive.
distractorRationale.b: Steroids mask peritonism; tachycardia is a red flag.
distractorRationale.c: Resuscitation is still required and imaging helps planning in a stable patient.
distractorRationale.d: A delay of 48 hours risks progression of untreated sepsis.

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression and corticosteroids blunt both pain and guarding, so a soft abdomen is falsely reassuring. A normal erect chest radiograph misses a proportion of perforations, so CT is the right next investigation alongside resuscitation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has pain that began around the umbilicus and moved to the RIF, vomiting, RIF tenderness, no rebound, temperature 37.0 degrees C, white cell count 13.2 x 10^9/L and neutrophils 82%. Using the Alvarado score as given in the lesson (migration 1, anorexia 1, nausea or vomiting 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 1, temperature above 37.3 degrees C 1, leucocytosis above 10 x 10^9/L 2, neutrophils above 75% 1), and noting he has no anorexia, calculate his score (points).
questions.explanation: Migration 1, anorexia 0, vomiting 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 0, temperature 0, leucocytosis 2 and neutrophilia 1 gives 1 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 7. A score of 7 or more is conventionally regarded as probable appendicitis, although cut-offs vary.

questions.stem: A 90 kg patient with peritonitis has a urinary catheter placed. Using the target of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h, what is the minimum acceptable hourly urine output, in mL/h?
questions.explanation: Target output is 0.5 mL per kg per hour multiplied by body weight: 0.5 x 90 = 45 mL/h. Persistently lower output suggests inadequate renal perfusion and the need for further resuscitation.

questions.stem: A normal white cell count and normal CRP reliably exclude acute appendicitis.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Blood markers are neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule out appendicitis, particularly early in the illness. Diagnosis rests on history, examination and, where needed, imaging, with serial review.

questions.stem: Explain, using the underlying pain pathways, why a patient with a right-sided inflamed gallbladder may report both right upper quadrant pain and right shoulder-tip pain, and how this differs from the pain of a simple gallstone obstructing the cystic duct without inflammation.
markingGuide: Gallbladder is a foregut structure: early visceral pain is dull and epigastric or right upper quadrant
Inflammation reaching parietal peritoneum gives sharp, localised RUQ pain worse on movement or inspiration
Diaphragmatic irritation referred through the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) causes right shoulder-tip pain
Biliary colic from cystic duct obstruction is visceral, colicky, episodic, without fever or peritonism
Cholecystitis is constant, longer than a few hours, with fever and Murphy's sign
questions.explanation: Visceral pain gives a vague foregut pain pattern, but when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum and diaphragm the pain becomes localised and referred to the shoulder tip. Simple biliary colic lacks inflammation, so it is episodic and without systemic signs.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of NSAID use has sudden epigastric pain and a board-like abdomen, heart rate 112/min and blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, and free gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest film. Outline your immediate resuscitation and the reasoning that leads to a decision for surgery.
markingGuide: ABC approach, oxygen if needed, two large-bore cannulae, bloods including lactate, cultures, group and save
Crystalloid bolus of 250 to 500 mL with reassessment rather than a fixed large volume
Early intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy
Analgesia, antiemetic, nil by mouth, urinary catheter with hourly output
Early senior surgical and anaesthetic involvement, ICU or HDU planning
Generalised peritonitis with shock needs source control (laparotomy or laparoscopy) after optimised, not prolonged, resuscitation
Imaging (erect chest radiograph or CT) only if it does not delay care
Weigh comorbidity, frailty and consent or best-interests discussion
questions.explanation: Generalised peritonitis with shock is a surgical emergency in which sepsis control depends on removing the source. Resuscitation and antibiotics begin immediately and run in parallel with decision-making by senior surgeons and anaesthetists.
